finding: Large multisite analysis identified cortical-predominant and subcortical-predominant neurostructural trajectories/subgroups across thousands of cases and controls; important positive evidence but not sufficient to resolve field-wide reproducibility concerns.

design: 12-month international multisite clinical cognitive functional digital study
finding: Three clinical-functional clusters were identified and framed as foundations for future validation rather than established diseases.
TRS shows recurring immune-inflammatory differences including cytokine and immune-cell findings, but clozapine/treatment effects and methodological heterogeneity limit etiologic interpretation.
Deficit schizophrenia showed poorer insight than nondeficit schizophrenia, strengthening clinical phenotype differentiation without establishing a separate etiologic disease.
Clozapine-versus-other-antipsychotic evidence reinforces a distinctive treatment pathway for TRS but treatment response alone does not establish ontology.
Biotype-specific transcriptomic signals and MR-prioritized genes add genetic coherence, while the Biotypes continue to cross schizophrenia, schizoaffective and bipolar psychosis boundaries.
Common-variant signal contributes to treatment-response heterogeneity but does not define a categorical TRS disease.
Polygenic liability relates to treatment complexity/resistance but remains distributed and overlapping rather than a single etiologic separator.

design: global rare-variant registry plus population comparison
finding: Pathogenic GRIN2A null variants confer high risk for early-onset psychiatric disorders including schizophrenia-spectrum psychosis and create a plausible precision-treatment subgroup; phenotype extends beyond schizophrenia.
Prospective ADEPT/B-SNIP-style testing is positioned to assess longitudinal and clinical utility of biotype assignment; outcome evidence is not yet available.
22q11.2 deletion syndrome confers major psychosis/schizophrenia risk and represents a genetically defined syndrome that can present with a schizophrenia phenotype; treatment evidence remains limited.

A small subset of first-episode psychosis has autoimmune encephalitis or clinically significant neural-autoimmune findings, supporting etiologic exclusion/subclassification when neurological or laboratory evidence is present.
Clinical risk stratification can enrich psychosis populations for antineuronal-antibody/autoimmune evaluation; this defines secondary etiologies rather than an idiopathic schizophrenia subtype.

design: genomic factor analysis 14 psychiatric disorders >1M cases
finding: Five genomic factors explained much shared psychiatric genetic variance; schizophrenia and bipolar disorder formed a highly overlapping factor with very few disorder-specific loci, weakening a clean schizophrenia-specific common-variant boundary.

design: cross-time fuzzy clustering plus independent local validation
finding: EF-Focal and EF-Global subtypes were longitudinally stable, differed in symptoms/inflammatory-metabolic markers, classified in an independent local sample (AUC 0.79), and predicted remission independently of baseline severity (AUC 0.78).

In 44 first-episode schizophrenia-spectrum patients, lower baseline CSF LDH plus early response predicted 5-year TRS with exploratory AUC 0.86; authors explicitly require larger independent validation.
Inflammatory signals associated with negative-symptom variation before established schizophrenia support early biology but are not schizophrenia-specific subtype evidence.
Negative symptoms constitute a reproducible treatment domain with differential intervention effects, but treatment-domain validity does not establish a separate disease.

design: CSF human biomarker plus experimental mechanistic work
finding: Low CACNA2D1-related signal was linked to schizophrenia cognitive/circuit abnormalities with experimental rescue evidence, strengthening a cognitive-mechanistic hypothesis but not yet a validated patient subtype.

finding: Rare pathogenic variants including CNVs and monogenic neurodevelopmental disorders can alter psychosis risk, medical surveillance and treatment considerations; they should be handled as etiologic diagnoses/subgroups rather than symptom subtypes.
